summary: This informational document lists requirements for a mechanism that lets a Path Computation Client dynamically and automatically discover Path Computation Elements, along with information useful for choosing among them. Solutions are expected to meet these requirements.

eli5.summary: Before asking a trip planner for help, you must find out which planners exist and what each is good at. This lists what a way of finding them must do.

subtitle: What an automatic way to find path computation servers in an MPLS or GMPLS network must be able to do.

tldr.problem: Clients that need a network path computed must know which Path Computation Elements exist, where they are and what they can do. Configuring that by hand on every client is heavy and cannot notice changes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements for a discovery mechanism: what PCE information must be disclosed, how far it spreads, how changes and failures are noticed, and how it is secured and managed.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document, not a protocol. Solutions that specify PCE discovery are expected to satisfy it.

today: RFC 4674 is an Informational requirements document with no listed obsoleting or updating RFCs. It sets out what a PCE discovery solution should satisfy and does not define a protocol itself.

sections.title: Why PCE Discovery Is Needed
sections.content:
In the PCE-based architecture of RFC 4655, a Path Computation Element (PCE) computes traffic-engineered label switched paths (TE-LSPs) from a network graph and a set of constraints. A Path Computation Client (PCC) is any client that asks a PCE for a path. A PCC can be a router asking for a path for which it is the head-end, or a PCE asking another PCE.

A PCC therefore has to know where one or more PCEs are in its own domain, and sometimes in other domains too. This document lists the functional requirements for a mechanism that does this automatically and dynamically. It does not choose a protocol, and it applies equally to MPLS-TE and GMPLS networks.
sections.eli5: Some helpers can work out the best route for you, but you have to know who they are first. This document says what a way of finding those helpers must be able to do.

sections.title: The Problem with Manual Configuration
sections.content:
A routing domain may contain many PCEs. Load can be shared among several for scalability, primary and backup PCEs can give redundancy, PCEs can differ in capability, and in an inter-domain setting each PCE may handle different inter-area, inter-AS or inter-layer work.

The PCC could be configured by hand with the list of PCEs. The RFC accepts that this can be sufficient or even preferred in some cases, for example inter-AS discovery where manual configuration of neighbor PCEs may be preferred for security reasons. But it adds configuration overhead, risks errors, and cannot tell a PCC that a PCE appeared, disappeared or changed. In a multi-area network where ABRs act as PCEs, the backbone area would hold at least N PCEs, and N can be beyond fifty.
sections.eli5: Writing down every helper's address on every computer is a lot of work and goes out of date fast. It is better if the computers can find the helpers on their own.

sections.title: Core Requirements and What Must Be Disclosed
sections.content:
The discovery mechanism MUST let a PCC automatically find PCEs in its domain and, where policy permits, in other domains. Disclosure is split in two levels.

  • General information (must be supported): the IPv4 and/or IPv6 address used to reach the PCE, the domains where it has visibility and can compute paths, and its inter-domain functions such as inter-area, inter-AS and inter-layer. Domains can be identified by an IGP area ID or an AS number.
  • Detailed information (may be supported): PCE capabilities and alternate PCEs.

Capabilities given as examples include link and path constraints, objective functions, diverse or load-balanced paths, bidirectional paths, maximum request size and computation power for weighted load balancing. Their exact definition is out of scope. A PCE may also name alternate PCEs to use if it fails.

Inter-domain functions are not always implied by visibility. A PCE seeing one domain may still help with inter-domain paths by cooperating with PCEs elsewhere, and a PCE seeing several domains may be barred by the operator from inter-domain use.
sections.eli5: Every helper must at least tell you where it is and which neighborhoods it knows. It may also say what special tricks it can do, and who covers for it when it is away.

sections.title: Scope, Change Detection and Policy
sections.content:
The mechanism MUST let the operator control, per PCE, who may learn about it. The choices must include at least all PCCs in a single IGP area, in a set of adjacent areas, in a single AS, in a set of ASs, or a set of PCCs in a set of ASs. Discovery MUST be configurable and be possible to deactivate per PCE.

PCCs MUST be able to learn that a new PCE appeared, that a known PCE changed, and that a PCE is no longer alive or was deactivated. Real-time detection is not required, but the mechanism SHOULD allow detection in a range of 60 seconds, and the operator should be able to configure the delay. PCE information is expected to be fairly static.

Policy MUST be supported to restrict scope to authorized domains, to control what is disclosed, and to filter and translate information at domain borders. Across AS borders it can make sense to disclose detailed capabilities only inside the PCE's own AS and just location and supported domains elsewhere.
sections.eli5: The owner of each helper decides who is allowed to know about it. Everyone who is allowed must find out fairly quickly when a helper arrives, changes or goes away.

sections.title: Security and Scalability Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC names five major threats: impersonation of a PCE, sniffing of discovery information, falsification of it, disclosure to unauthorized PCCs (PCC spoofing) and denial of service. Security is described as especially important between ASs. Mechanisms MUST exist to authenticate discovery information, verify its integrity, encrypt it, and restrict its scope to authorized PCCs. PCEs and PCCs MUST have globally unique IDs, for instance an AS number combined with an IP address, and the mechanism MUST explicitly support a set of trust models.

On scale, the mechanism MUST scale with the number of PCCs, PCEs and domains, and MUST NOT hurt other protocols such as routing and signaling. Minimum orders of magnitude are 1000 PCCs discovering a given PCE and 100 PCEs discovered by a given PCC. The mechanism MUST also be extensible so new PCE information can be added later. The RFC's own Security Considerations section says that, being a requirements document, it raises no particular security issue by itself.
sections.eli5: Because helpers tell others about themselves, a trickster might pretend to be one or read private notes. So the system must check who is who, keep messages secret, and not fall over if someone floods it.

sections.title: Manageability Requirements
sections.content:
Mechanisms are REQUIRED to manage PCE discovery. It MUST be possible to enable and disable discovery on both PCCs and PCEs, and turning on automatic discovery MUST NOT block static configuration that adds to what was discovered. Configuration may be through a local interface or a standard one such as a MIB module.

MIB modules MUST be specified for PCCs and PCEs. The PCC module has to expose the known PCEs, the discovered and locally configured data for each, and how long ago each was discovered or changed. The PCE module has to expose a control to disable announcements, the advertised information and the active policies.

Operators MUST also be able to monitor the protocol and to limit the impact of frequent changes, for example with a configurable limit on how fast changed parameters are announced and control of what makes a PCC swap to another PCE.
sections.eli5: People running the network need dials and gauges. They must be able to switch the finding feature on or off, see what has been found, and stop it from causing a fuss when things change a lot.
